opus-5.5.text:
I think "sculpting" is a good word for it, because a lot of architecture work really is like that. You start with a big block of material, which these days is basically the Transformer, and you carve away at it, or reshape parts of it, to get something more efficient or more expressive. I have mixed feelings about it.

On the positive side, I think it's a very healthy way to do research when it's grounded in principles. In my own work on linear attention and things like DeltaNet, we weren't just randomly trying modules. We asked very concrete questions. What is attention actually doing? What does a recurrent state need to store? Why does vanilla linear attention fail at associative recall? Once you frame it as an online learning or memory-update problem, the delta rule falls out naturally: you're doing a step of gradient descent on the state to correct what's already stored, instead of just piling things on. Then gating is another principled knob, because it controls forgetting. So in that sense the sculpting is guided by a clear mental model, and I think that kind of work tends to last.

What I'm more skeptical of is sculpting for its own sake. You add a little convolution here, a gate there, change the normalization, and you get half a point on some benchmark at a small scale. The problem is that many of these tweaks don't survive scaling, and they don't survive contact with real hardware. An architecture that looks elegant on paper but can't be trained efficiently on GPUs is, practically speaking, dead. That's why I care so much about hardware-efficient algorithms, like chunkwise parallel forms that make good use of tensor cores. For me, an architectural idea isn't finished until you can show it trains fast at scale.

I'd also say the Transformer itself is a good lesson. It wasn't the most expressive or theoretically beautiful design. It won largely because it was simple and extremely parallelizable. So when people sculpt new architectures, I think the real test is whether you're removing something that's actually unnecessary, or adding something that's actually necessary, in a way the hardware is happy with. Hybrid models are a good example of that. Mixing a few global attention layers with many efficient linear-recurrent layers is a fairly pragmatic piece of sculpting, and it seems to work really well in practice.

So overall I'm in favor, but I'd want the chisel guided by understanding, both of what the model needs to compute and of what the hardware can do efficiently, rather than by benchmark chasing.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "sculpting" is actually a pretty honest description of what architecture work looks like day to day, but it can also be misleading if people take it too literally.

The honest part is that nobody sits down and derives an architecture from first principles. You start with something that works, like softmax attention, and you ask what's actually load-bearing in it. Then you chip away: can I replace the softmax with a linear kernel? Can I add a gate? A decay term? A delta rule instead of a plain accumulate? Each change is small, and you measure, and most of them don't help. So it really does feel like carving, where the shape emerges from many small cuts rather than from one big idea.

The misleading part is the image of a sculptor with a clear vision who just removes whatever doesn't belong. In practice, we don't know what the final statue looks like. The feedback loop is empirical: you train at small scale, you look at loss curves, you look at retrieval and in-context tasks, and you keep what survives. A lot of ideas that look elegant on paper die at 1B parameters. And a lot of things that look like hacks, like a scalar decay or a specific normalization placement, turn out to matter more than the "principled" component you were proud of.

So the way I try to work is to anchor the sculpting in something more structured. For linear attention and state-space style models, I find it useful to think in terms of what the recurrent state is actually doing. Is it a key-value associative memory? What's the write rule, what's the forget rule, what's the read rule? Once you frame it that way, a lot of architectures that look different on the surface, Mamba, RetNet, GLA, DeltaNet, are just different choices in that same small design space. Then "sculpting" becomes less random: you're not guessing, you're deliberately moving along a few axes and asking what each axis buys you.

The other thing I'd say is that the sculpting is constrained by hardware more than people admit. An operation that looks beautiful mathematically but can't be chunked and run as matmuls on a GPU is basically dead. So a lot of my work has been making sure that the architectures we want are also the ones that can be trained efficiently, because otherwise the empirical loop I just described never closes. You can't sculpt what you can't train.

So: yes, it's sculpting, but I'd want the sculptor to have a theory of the material, and to be using tools that actually cut.

astra-6.text:
I think “sculpting” an architecture can be useful, but the question is what’s guiding the changes. Are you addressing a limitation you understand, or are you trying variations until the benchmark improves? Both can produce results, but they give you different kinds of knowledge.

For me, the interesting part is identifying the principle behind a successful design. Why does this structure help? Does the benefit survive changes in scale, data, or training setup? Can you simplify it and retain the improvement? If you can answer those questions, you’ve learned something that may carry over to the next model. Otherwise, you may have a very carefully tuned architecture without knowing which details actually matter.

So I wouldn’t dismiss architectural craftsmanship. Experimentation often comes before understanding. But I’d treat a successful modification as the beginning of an explanation, rather than the end of the work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “sculpting” an architecture is really about choosing the right inductive biases. You’re deciding what structure to build into the model and what to leave for it to learn from data. That can be valuable, especially when you have limited data or a clear computational constraint.

But it’s easy to become attached to an elegant design. A module might make intuitive sense without actually improving the model. So I’d treat architectural ideas as hypotheses: compare them against a simple baseline, control the training conditions, and see whether the benefit survives changes in scale and data.

For me, the goal isn’t to make the architecture look sophisticated. It’s to find the simplest structure that gives you a meaningful, reproducible advantage.
